title: Race relations in Sherman while he was growing up
summary: Segregated but friendly neighbours; he played with a white band in Sherman about 1933.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Before we get back to the chronology, I wanted -- what was the racial situation like in Sherman?
Yeah. When you were growing up.
Well, you couldn't go -- you know, like we couldn't integrate, you know, like we couldn't go to places. But they treated us very well.
The black communities and the white communities were very separate.

Yeah, but you know, in my home town, this is what I talk about today. They all, white and black, lived next door to each other. And they still do. Now, maybe I live here and two door -- next door would be a white family and there would be a black family in there. They always did that in Sherman, Texas. Of course, they had a terrible thing happen there. They burned the courthouse down there once because they brought a guy there for safekeeping and they followed him on, you know, from another town. That was a very bad mark for the town. But the town actually was a good town, really, and we always got along all right and I even used to play -- I played with a white band in Sherman right around in 1932 or 3. Not many jobs, but I went on and played some jobs with them, I came on home and I played a couple gigs with them and you know, they wasn't doing things like that then. This was back like in '33. And those guys are still my friends, some of them are lawyers and one's a lawyer -- the leader of the band's a lawyer and he's in Washington and they're all scattered out like that.
So it really wasn't too bad. You just -- you knew
you were segregated and you were used to it. But we had our own things, you know. We would own theaters, own ballrooms.
